articles.body: It was during the final ten minutes of a Jumu'ah prayer. The mosque was silent, save for the soft cadence of the imam. Suddenly, a sharp, upbeat ringtone cut through the stillness like a knife. Every head turned. The person responsible didn't just look embarrassed; they looked devastated. I sat there, phone in my pocket, and realized I had been that person exactly three weeks prior during a high-stakes job interview. We all have these moments where our devices fail to respect the environment, and we simply forget to manage our own volume. The problem The fundamental issue is that humans are terrible at context-switching. We are expected to remember to silence our phones before entering a meeting, then remember to turn them back up afterward.

articles.title: Verify Webhook Signatures in Request Inspector
articles.excerpt: Webhook handlers often reject valid payloads with an HTTP 400 or 401 during local development. A trailing newline in an environment variable, a JSON body parsed before verification, or a signing secre…
articles.body: Webhook handlers often reject valid payloads with an HTTP 400 or 401 during local development. A trailing newline in an environment variable, a JSON body parsed before verification, or a signing secret copied from the wrong place is enough to break a signature check. Triggering live events from a provider dashboard over and over is a slow way to find out which one it was. A tunnel with a request inspector gives you the method, path, headers, status and (if you keep it) body of each delivery. This guide covers why signature checks fail, what each provider sends, how to check signatures with the InstaWormhole Request Inspector, and how to replay a captured request after you fix your handler.

articles.title: WAF Filtering vs CMS File Validation: Where Upload Controls Belong
articles.excerpt: A CMS upload endpoint is a path from an untrusted client to persistent storage. If an attacker can turn an uploaded file into executable server code, that path can become web shell access. The securit…
articles.body: A CMS upload endpoint is a path from an untrusted client to persistent storage. If an attacker can turn an uploaded file into executable server code, that path can become web shell access. The security decision is therefore bigger than whether a request looks suspicious: who decides what may be stored, and what prevents that stored object from running? For teams deciding how to block malicious file uploads on a CMS, compare two configuration choices: concentrating enforcement at the reverse proxy, or combining proxy filtering with strict CMS acceptance and storage rules. The second gives each layer a decision it can actually support. Choice A: Concentrate upload enforcement at the WAF A WAF operates before the CMS handles a request.
articles.author: 禾

articles.title: How to Block Malicious File Uploads on a CMS Before They Become Web Shells
articles.excerpt: A CMS upload feature can become a route to server execution when it accepts a dangerous file and stores it somewhere the server can execute it. An attacker may submit a script disguised as an image, e…
articles.body: A CMS upload feature can become a route to server execution when it accepts a dangerous file and stores it somewhere the server can execute it. An attacker may submit a script disguised as an image, exploit a vulnerable plugin's upload endpoint, or use a stolen editor account to reach a restricted media workflow. If the uploaded file becomes a web shell, subsequent HTTP requests can turn it into a command interface. For security owners asking how to block malicious file uploads on a CMS, the practical answer combines application validation, storage isolation, access controls, and traffic filtering.

articles.title: How sci‑fi imagines sports in microgravity, and how zero‑g sports might actually work
articles.excerpt: How realistic are the zero-g sports we see in sci-fi? We talk to Les Johnson, former Chief Technologist for NASA, to find out.
articles.body: Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing after launching into suborbital space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit.

articles.body: Encapsulate Inc. This Nov. 19, 2026, image shows gastric microtumors grown within an Encapsulates biochip. The Encapsulate-1 investigation studies patient-derived tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to better understand how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. The results could help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments. Orbiting more than 200 miles (320 km) above Earth, the space station is a powerhouse of cutting-edge science that is unlocking discoveries not possible on Earth. Image credit: Encapsulate Inc.
